blocks.p: Dear Stephen, the salvage tug blew a seal on the way back from Lagrange today. For ninety seconds every one of us aboard believed we were dead, and I found that I wanted very badly to pray, and did not know to whom. I am writing it down so that you cannot pretend afterward that it was otherwise.
The Petrel came apart somewhere between one star and the next, and Sol Tarren slept through it.

He woke to red light and a sound like a kettle left too long on a stove. The lid of his pod was open. That was the first wrong thing. On every crossing he had ever made he had woken under glass, with a steward’s face coming into focus above him. Now there was no glass, only a ceiling set at an angle no ceiling should have, and a strip of emergency light along it, pulsing slow and red, and cold. Not the sealed cold of stasis. This cold moved. It came from somewhere and went somewhere, and it smelled of struck matches.
He tried to sit up, and his body did not obey at once. That was not new; for a year now his knees had had to be asked twice. He got an elbow under him and looked.

The passenger hold of the Petrel lay tilted like a boat on a beach. The two rows of pods ran downhill, and at the low end the bulkhead was gone. In its place was a ragged mouth of torn metal, its edges curled outward like the petals of some terrible flower, and beyond it was a sky the brown-red of an old bruise. A third of it was filled by a planet. It hung there enormous and close, banded in rust and ochre and wine, and the bands moved: slow storms the size of worlds, turning against each other. Below it lay a plain of black sand that glittered dully, and here and there across the plain stood white plumes of steam, rising straight and slow into the windless air.
“Sol.”
Teo was crouched at the end of the row with a hand lamp, his face streaked with something dark. The boy’s voice was steady in the way a voice is steady when its owner has decided it must be.

“The hold came down on its own,” Teo said. “It’s built to. Thorne rule: the passengers ride in a lifeboat. It flew itself down to the nearest air and woke everybody on the way.” He swallowed. “Most everybody. Some pods lost power when we hit. Tobin’s opening them by hand.”
“Where are we?”
“I don’t know yet.” Teo’s eyes went past him, to the pod on Sol’s left, and something in his face gave way. “Sol. It’s Lyda.”
Her pod had not opened.

Its glass had cracked in a long star from one corner, and frost had grown inside the crack, thick and white, so that he could see her only in pieces: a hand, a strand of dark hair stiff with ice, the curve of a cheek gone the color of candle wax. The panel at the pod’s head, which should have shown three green lights, showed nothing at all.

Lucan was already there. The doctor was in his shirtsleeves with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead and his small leather case open on the deck, and he was working the manual release with both thumbs, his lips moving. He was counting. Lucan counted when he was frightened.

“The pod lost power in the break,” Lucan said, without looking up. “The implant should have carried her through it. That is what it is for. It should have kept her heart going and woken her when the lid failed.” The release gave. “It is the first one I ever built.”
Together they lifted the lid. Lyda lay in the cold with her eyes half open and her lips blue, and she did not breathe.

Sol had seen the dead. He had laid two fingers on the temples of thirty-one thousand of them, and kept the count, and sent them up into Life, and they had all looked like this, a little, as though someone had gone out of a room and left the lamp burning. He had never been afraid of them.
“Out,” Lucan said. “Flat on the deck. Gently. Her heart will be like glass.”

She weighed nothing. The gravity here was light, about the pull of Mars, and she came up out of the pod as though she were floating in water. They laid her on the tilted deck on Sol’s coat. Lucan put two fingers to her throat and held them there a long time. Then he put his ear to her chest.
“Nothing,” he said. He sat back on his heels. “She is very cold.”
“Do something.”

“I am thinking.” Lucan’s voice was precise and quiet. “There is an old rule. It was old before the Tragedy. No one is dead until they are warm and dead.” He looked at Sol. “Kneel there. Heel of your hand here, on the bone, the other hand over it. Lock your arms. Push hard and fast, twice a second, as deep as the width of your thumb. You will feel things break. Do not stop when they do.”

Sol knelt, and put his hands where Lucan put them, and pushed, and nothing happened except that he rose. In the light gravity the push lifted him off his own knees. He braced one knee against the frame of the pod and tried again, and this time he went down with his whole weight, and he felt it under the heel of his hand, a small soft crack like a green branch.
“Good,” Lucan said. “Again. Count aloud.”

He counted. Lucan bent and breathed into her mouth, twice, and sat back, and Sol counted again. Somewhere down the row Tobin forced another lid, and someone woke screaming. Teo came back from the forward locker with a grey box, and Lucan opened it, and inside were two flat pads and a dial.
“Thorne ships carry them,” Teo said. “People still die out here.”
“Hands off her.”

Lucan laid the pads on her, and the box spoke in a flat voice, and her whole body jumped once on the deck and came down slowly in the light gravity, the way the old man had come down in the market. Lucan listened.
“Nothing. Push.”

Sol pushed. His shoulders began to burn and then to shake. He was not a young man any longer; he had not been one for a year. He kept pushing. The box spoke again, and she jumped again, and Lucan listened, and shook his head.
“Tarren,” Lucan said, after the third time. His voice had changed. “It has been a long while.”
“No.”
“Her heart was cold for too...”
“No.”

He did not know he was praying until he heard himself. It was not a good prayer. It was only words between the counts. It was Tobin’s prayer, from the floor of the residence at Concord, and it was the only one he had. Lord, you said. Here she is. Here she is.
Lucan put the pads on her a fourth time. He did not look as though he expected anything. The box spoke.
She jumped, and came down, and lay still.
Then she coughed.

It was a terrible sound, wet and tearing, and her body curled around it, and Lucan was at her throat and then at her chest, and he said, “There. There it is. Oh, there it is,” in a voice Sol had never heard him use, and sat back on the deck and took his spectacles off and put his hand over his eyes.

Sol knelt with his hands open in the air above her, as though she were something he had just let go of. Her eyes moved under the lids. Her breath came in short, shallow pulls, as if each one had to be argued for.

“Warm her,” Lucan said, behind his hand. “Slowly. Bodies, not lamps. Her heart will not stand a shock.” He took his hand away. His eyes were wet, and he did not seem to notice. “And someone write down the time. I want to know how long she was gone.”
Teo told him about the aft section while Lyda slept between Tobin and the wall, wrapped in every blanket the hold held, the big man’s arms around her like a crate around something fragile.

The crew had ridden aft, by the drive, so that they would be first to it on waking. Corwin Brack, master of the Petrel for thirty years, who had known the Thornes’ father. Ina Moss, the navigator, who sang on the gangway. The engineer, Fenn, a quiet man who had once shown Sol how to read a pressure gauge and seemed embarrassed to be thanked. When the ship broke, the aft section had gone one way and the hold another. The hold had found air and come down. The aft section had not.

“I was supposed to be back there,” Teo said. He sat against a pod, turning the lamp over in his fingers. “Crew ride aft. Lyda wouldn’t let me. She said a hand who isn’t let near the stick can ride with the cargo like everyone else, and we fought about it on the gangway in front of Ina.” He stopped turning the lamp. “Ina laughed at me.”

Sol sat down beside him. His knees complained. He said nothing, because nothing in all his years of the gift had taught him what to say, and because he had learned this past year that sometimes there was nothing, and that it was all right.
“Are they in Life?” Teo said at last. “Brack was renewed. Ina too. Fenn wasn’t anything; he hated the church. Are they...”
“I don’t know,” Sol said. “I used to know. I used to say it every day.”

Teo put his face down on his knees, and his shoulders shook, and Sol put an arm around him, and the boy wept against his side without any shame at all. A miner from the forward rows, a renewed man with an untouched face, looked away quickly, as if he had seen something indecent. Sol let him look away. He held the boy and grieved with him for a woman who had sung on the gangway, and the light pulsed red along the ceiling, and outside the broken hull the great banded planet turned.

They counted themselves before the light went. Thirty-four were living. Lucan splinted a leg with a strip of pod frame and closed a scalp by lamplight, in his dry clinic voice. The first mate, Dorran Kade, had come down with the passengers by the luck of being late to his own pod, and he took up the command he had been left like a man taking up a load.

The deckhand who knew the place was called Pim. He had been late to the aft pods with Kade, and was alive for the same reason. He was young and thin and renewed, and he had worked two seasons at a sulfur station on this moon.

“It’s Viper,” he said. He said it the way a man names an illness. “The big one up there’s the Coil. The station’s on the far side, three hundred kilometers or more. They’ll hear a beacon, if the beacon works.” He looked out at the black plain. “In two hours we go into the Coil’s shadow. Eleven hours of it. It gets cold enough to stop your breath. You need a fire, and you need to stay off the sand after dark. Adders. They live down in the warm cracks and come out for heat. That’s why it’s called Viper. Nobody gets up from one. I saw a man bitten my first season. He was dead by the morning shift.”

The cargo forward of the pods was timber, long crates of cured blackwood from the hill country up the Wend, bound for the yards at Galatia. Kade had them break it up. They built the fire in the lee of the hull, where a fissure in the sand breathed out a warm, sour steam, and when Teo struck it the flames went up tall and slow in the light gravity, and the sparks rose so high and so lazily that the children who were still awake reached up for them as though they were stars.

Sol watched the sparks go up, and the bone behind his left eye ached once, lightly, and eased. For the space of a breath there was no fire. There was a room with the lights turned off and a door opening, and a woman coming through it with a cake held out in front of her, its candles making a small moving cave of light around her face. She was grinning, and there was a gap between her front teeth, and the whole dark room was singing, badly, and laughing at itself for singing. Then there was only the fire again, and the sparks, and the black plain.
Lucan, kneeling by the man with the splinted leg, had seen his face. “Was that one?”
“Only the edge of one.” Sol looked into the flames. “Somebody’s birthday.”
Lucan wrote it down.
Then the Coil’s shadow came over them.

It crossed the plain like a tide. The far plumes went grey and then went out, and the dark was on them and the cold with it, and Sol understood at once why Pim had said what he said. It was not the cold of Serenity, a cold that had been there a billion years and expected nothing. This cold was hungry. It came at the back of his neck and between his shoulders, and the air went thin and sharp in his throat, and the only warmth in the world was the ring of the fire and the bodies pressed close around it.

Lyda was awake. They had carried her out in her blankets and set her nearest the flames, propped against Tobin, her face grey in the firelight. Lucan had forbidden her to speak. But she found Sol’s eyes across the fire and held them, and he saw her mouth move on his name.
He went to get more wood.

The broken crates were stacked at the edge of the light, near the mouth of the fissure. He crouched and pulled a slat loose, then another, gathering them against his chest, his hands clumsy with cold. He reached for a long piece lying half in the warm mouth of the crack, and closed his hand on it, and something closed on his hand.

It came out of the steam all at once, the length of a man’s forearm, black and slick and glittering like the sand, and it struck him between the thumb and first finger and held on. He felt two points of heat go into him like nails. Someone cried out behind him. He stood up with the thing hanging from his hand, its body whipping slow and heavy in the light gravity, and looked at it. It had no eyes he could see. Its jaw was locked in the meat of his hand, and it was pumping something into him. He could feel the rhythm of it.
He walked to the fire and shook his hand over the flames, once, hard. The thing let go and fell into the coals, and writhed there, and was still.
No one around the fire said anything. Thirty-three faces looked at him in the red light. Pim had gone white.
“Show me,” Lucan said.
There were two punctures in the web of the hand, small and neat, a bead of dark blood welling from each. Lucan turned it to the light and pressed the skin around them with his thumb, and frowned.
“Does it burn?”
“A little.”
“Any numbness? Lips, tongue?”
“No.”

Lucan cleaned it and bound it and wrote something in the little book he carried in his breast pocket. Then he sat down beside Sol and took his wrist and held it, his eyes on the watch he had laid on his knee, and did not let go.
They all watched him. Sol felt it all through the shadow, all eleven hours of it: thirty-three people waiting for him to swell, or burn, or fall down dead. Every time Sol shifted, Pim flinched.
The voice came sometime after the middle of the night.

You brought her, it said, in his own voice, with the crackle under it like sleet. She would have stayed home. You brought her into the cold and she died, she died, she died on the deck and you could not even let her stay dead. Everything you touch. The boy in the mud at Reedmouth. Hob’s arm. Brack and Moss and Fenn. Everything you touch. Everything...

He opened his mouth to answer it and found that the cold had got into the word. It would not come. He sat with his bitten hand in his lap and the voice going on and on in him, and could not find the one thing he had always been able to find.
Teo was watching him across the fire. Perhaps it showed. The boy got up and came round and sat down hard against his side, and said it for him, quietly, the way you hand a man a tool he has dropped.
“Christ.”
The voice came apart like wet paper. Lucan glanced at the two of them and said nothing, and wrote something else in the little book.

Sol began to say the psalm then. It was simply there, as Stephen had said it would be: the one Stephen had said to him from a cot, and that he had found whole in the grey notebook on Daphne and read until the page went soft. He said it under his breath, and then a little louder, because Teo was close against him and listening. The Lord is my shepherd. I have all that I need. He makes me lie down in green pastures. (Ps. 23:1–2) There were no green pastures anywhere on Viper. There was black glass and a sky like a bruise and a cold that wanted them dead. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. (Ps. 23:4) Across the fire, against Tobin’s chest, Lyda had closed her eyes, and her lips were moving with his. She knew only the pieces Teo had said on floors. She was following the shape of the rest, the way he had once followed the shape of a line spoken in a market on Mars.

Morning on Viper was the rim of the Coil coming back into the sun. It came slowly, a thin bright edge along the planet’s curve, and then the light ran down across the black plain, and the plumes of steam lit up white one after another, like candles being lit along a nave.
Sol’s hand was stiff and sore. It was nothing else.

Pim came around the fire and stood in front of him. He looked at the bandaged hand, and then at Sol’s face, and there was something in his own face that Sol knew well. He had seen it every day of his old life, in the cathedral at Abundance. It was the way people looked at the Pearls in their homes.
“You’re one of the bishops,” Pim said. “They said so on the ship. The bishops can’t die.”

“I’m not a bishop,” Sol said. “And I can die, Pim. I’m dark. Look at me.” He held up his hands, the grey in the hair on the backs of them, the knuckles beginning to thicken. “I’ll die like anyone. Only not last night.”
Pim did not look as though he believed it. He went back to his place, and Sol saw him lean over and whisper to Kade, and saw Kade look across at him, and away.
“I would very much like to know what was in that animal,” Lucan said, closing his book. “And why it did not do to you what it did to Pim’s man.”
“So would I.”
“You will tell me if you think of an answer.”
“You’ll be the first.”

Teo had gone back into the wreck at first light. He came out now, picking his way down the tilted deck with a slab of grey hardware under his arm, trailing cut wires. The beacon was working, he said. It was running off the hold’s last cell, and it would run a week, and the station would hear it.

But he did not sit down. He stood at the edge of the fire with the hardware in his arms, looking from Sol to his sister and back, with the face of a boy who has found something he does not want to have found.
“It’s the nav core,” he said. “I wanted to know where we were.” He wet his lips. “Sol, the turn wasn’t supposed to be here. We were never supposed to come anywhere near this moon.”
